blocks.title: Combining it all into one goal

summary.title: Four trainable qualities
points: Strength: the force you can produce. Hypertrophy: muscle growth.
Muscular endurance: how long or how often a muscle keeps working.
Mobility: active, controlled range of motion; flexibility is passive range.
Aerobic fitness is the engine around them all (Module 7).
They overlap; your goal sets the emphasis.

exercises.scenario: You can hold a deep squat only if someone pushes you down into it.

questions.prompt: Which quality is limited?
options: Aerobic fitness
Mobility
Flexibility, since that's the active, controlled range
Hypertrophy, because the legs are too small
questions.explanation: Passive range exists; active control doesn't yet.

questions.prompt: 'The heaviest weight you can lift once' describes which quality?
options: Power
Hypertrophy
Maximal strength
Muscular endurance over many repetitions
questions.explanation: Measured as a 1RM.

exercises.scenario: Your goals are fat loss, muscle and strength.

questions.prompt: Which qualities will your sessions mainly train?
options: Mobility only
Muscular endurance only, with very high reps every session
Power only
Hypertrophy and strength
questions.explanation: Mobility and core go in the warm-up; sport covers endurance.

questions.prompt: Does training for muscle also build strength?
options: Yes, the qualities overlap
No, they need completely separate programmes
Only after a year
Only if you lift on a machine
questions.explanation: Emphasis, not exclusion.

summary.title: Strength vs muscle: the rep ranges
points: Muscle grows across about 6–30 reps per set when sets end close to failure.
Very light loads (~20% 1RM) build less muscle.
Strength grows best with heavier loads: ≥ ~80% of 1RM, 2–3 sets (ACSM 2026).
Muscle: about 10 sets per muscle group per week.
Light dumbbells still build muscle; heavy lower-body strength needs heavier kit.

exercises.scenario: You can do 25 hard goblet squats with your heaviest weight.

questions.prompt: What does that set best build?
options: Nothing; it's too light to matter
Muscle and muscular endurance
Power, because the set is long
Maximal strength, as long as you do several sets of it
questions.explanation: Close to failure at 15–30 reps builds muscle, not max strength.

questions.prompt: You want leg strength. What's the implication?
options: Nothing: more reps with the same weight build maximal strength just as well
Stretch more before squatting
You'll need a heavier kettlebell or dumbbells
Do the squats faster
questions.explanation: Strength needs heavier loads.

exercises.scenario: A friend insists 'you must do exactly 8–12 reps to grow muscle'.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence say?
options: Only 8–12 reps builds muscle; anything else is endurance work
Rep range doesn't matter, even far from failure
Only sets of 1–5 reps build muscle
Muscle grows across a wide range if sets are near failure
questions.explanation: Effort and weekly sets matter more.

questions.prompt: About how many weekly sets per muscle group does ACSM 2026 suggest for growth?
options: About 10
About 2, as long as each set goes to complete failure
About 30
About 50
questions.explanation: Across a wide range of loads.

summary.title: Fat loss and lifting
points: Fat goes down when energy out exceeds energy in over weeks: a calorie deficit.
Food decides most of the balance; exercise adds to energy out.
Lifting in a deficit protects lean mass and keeps strength gains.
Deficits of ~500 kcal/day or more stalled lean-mass gains (2022 meta-analysis).
Aim to lose about 0.5–1% of body weight a week.

exercises.scenario: You weigh 80 kg and want to lose fat while keeping muscle.

questions.prompt: What's a sensible weekly pace?
options: About 0.4–0.8 kg
About 0.1 kg
About 2 kg, since faster loss keeps motivation high and muscle follows
As fast as possible
questions.explanation: 0.5–1% of body weight a week.

questions.prompt: Two people lose 5 kg on the same diet; one also lifts. What's likely?
options: The lifter can eat without limits
The lifter loses less fat overall
The lifter loses more fat and less muscle
No difference, since weight lost is weight lost whatever you do
questions.explanation: Lifting signals the body to keep muscle.

exercises.scenario: You plan to cut 1,000 kcal a day to speed things up.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk?
options: Fat loss stops completely
Muscle gain stalls and training suffers
Strength doubles
None, as long as you keep training hard every day
questions.explanation: Large deficits stalled lean-mass gains.

questions.prompt: Why does food matter more than exercise for the deficit?
options: Food is the only thing that affects weight
Exercise doesn't use any energy at all
Lifting adds calories to the body
It's far easier to eat 300 kcal than to burn them
questions.explanation: Exercise helps, but intake decides most of it.

summary.title: Cardio vs weights
points: Cardio uses more energy per session and builds the heart and lungs.
Weights build and keep muscle, strength and bone.
STRRIDE AT/RT: cardio lost more fat, weights added lean mass, both did both at ~2× the time.
WHO: 150–300 min moderate aerobic a week, plus muscle strengthening on ≥2 days.
Your sport covers much of the aerobic part.

exercises.scenario: You play sport twice a week and want to meet the WHO guidelines.

questions.prompt: What's missing?
options: Nothing at all
More aerobic minutes, since sport doesn't count as activity
Muscle-strengthening on at least 2 days
Daily stretching
questions.explanation: Sport covers much of the aerobic part.

questions.prompt: Which type best protects muscle in a deficit?
options: Stretching
Resistance training
Long, slow cardio sessions done several times a week
Walking only
questions.explanation: Weights add or keep lean mass.

exercises.scenario: A friend asks 'cardio or weights for fat loss?'

questions.prompt: What did STRRIDE AT/RT show?
options: Both together: fat loss plus lean mass
No difference between any groups
Cardio alone added the most lean mass
Weights alone lost the most fat in the trial
questions.explanation: At about twice the training time.

questions.prompt: What's the WHO aerobic minimum for adults?
options: There's no aerobic guideline
30 min of vigorous activity a week is enough for adults
60 min a day of running
150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous a week
questions.explanation: Plus muscle strengthening on ≥2 days.

summary.title: Mixing cardio and lifting
points: Concurrent training: endurance and strength in one programme.
2021 meta-analysis: no reduction in muscle growth or maximal strength.
Small reduction in explosive strength when sessions were within 20 minutes.
No effect at ≥3 hours apart; order made no clear difference.
For football and tennis: keep strength ≥3 h from sport and hard legs away from match days.

exercises.scenario: You play tennis Tuesday evening and want a strength session that day.

questions.prompt: When's best?
options: During the tennis warm-up
Straight after tennis, within 20 minutes, while you're warm
Never in the same week as tennis
Tuesday morning, at least 3 hours before
questions.explanation: Spacing protects explosive strength.

questions.prompt: You have a match Saturday. Where does the hard leg session go?
options: Not on Friday
Saturday morning before the match
Saturday evening straight after
Friday, so the legs are freshly stimulated for the match
questions.explanation: Keep hard leg work away from match days.

exercises.scenario: A gym friend says 'cardio kills your gains'.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence say?
options: Any cardio cancels all muscle growth from lifting
Only cycling interferes
No effect on muscle size or max strength
Cardio doubles strength gains
questions.explanation: Small effect only on explosive strength.

questions.prompt: Did lifting before or after cardio matter?
options: Yes, always lift first or gains are lost
No clear difference
Yes, always do cardio first
Only for people over 40
questions.explanation: Order had no clear effect.

summary.title: Losing fat and gaining muscle
points: Body recomposition: losing fat and gaining muscle at once.
Most likely in people new to lifting, returning, or with more body fat.
It needs enough protein and progressive resistance training.
Keep the deficit moderate; large deficits stall muscle gain.
Judge by waist, photos and strength as well as the scale.

exercises.scenario: After 8 weeks: weight unchanged, waist −3 cm, push-ups 15 → 22.

questions.prompt: What's most likely?
options: Recomposition
A broken scale
Nothing; the programme isn't working
Only water loss, which will come back within a week
questions.explanation: Less fat, more muscle, same weight.

questions.prompt: What would most likely stall it?
options: Adding reps each week
Eating enough protein every day
Measuring the waist
A crash diet
questions.explanation: Large deficits stop muscle gain.

exercises.scenario: You've played sport for years but never lifted seriously.

questions.prompt: Are you a good candidate for recomposition?
options: Only with supplements
Yes: new to lifting
Only if you stop all sport
No: recomposition only happens in trained bodybuilders
questions.explanation: Beginners to lifting respond well.

questions.prompt: Which two things does it always need?
options: Stretching and sleep only
Supplements and machines
Enough protein and progressive resistance training
A large deficit and daily long runs
questions.explanation: Module 9 covers protein.

summary.title: Setting your 12-week goal
points: One priority leads each 12-week block.
Mix outcome, performance and behaviour targets.
Behaviour targets are the ones you control: sessions, steps, protein.
Use your baseline for the numbers.
Review at weeks 4, 8 and 12.

exercises.scenario: You write your goal card.

questions.prompt: Which is a behaviour target?
options: 25 push-ups by week 12
Looking leaner in photos
A waist that's 4 cm smaller by the end of the 12 weeks
Three 30-minute sessions a week
questions.explanation: It's an action you control.

questions.prompt: Where do your performance numbers come from?
options: An online chart of averages for people of your age
A friend's results
Your baseline tests
Last year's guesses
questions.explanation: Compare with yourself.

exercises.scenario: Week 4: you hit 3 sessions every week, but the waist hasn't moved.

questions.prompt: What do you do?
options: Keep going and check food and steps at the review
Abandon the plan and start a completely new one
Stop tracking the waist
Double the number of sessions immediately
questions.explanation: Behaviour is on track; adjust the next lever.

questions.prompt: Why have one priority per block?
options: Because goals can't be measured otherwise
It decides what gets the best slot when time is short
Because the body can only change one quality per year
Because the WHO requires it
questions.explanation: With 3 × 30 minutes, you can't chase everything at full speed.

summary.title: Qualities, loads and fat loss
points: Strength, hypertrophy, muscular endurance and mobility overlap; goals set the emphasis.
Muscle grows across ~6–30 reps near failure; strength needs heavier loads.
ACSM 2026: ~10 sets per muscle a week for growth; ≥80% 1RM for strength.
Fat loss needs a moderate deficit; lifting keeps the muscle.
Lose about 0.5–1% of body weight a week.

exercises.scenario: Your kit: 12 kg kettlebell, dumbbells up to 10 kg. Goals: fat loss, muscle, strength.

questions.prompt: What can this kit do well now?
options: Nothing useful until you buy more
Build maximal leg strength, as long as you add enough sets
Build muscle with sets taken close to failure
Only cardio
questions.explanation: Light loads near failure grow muscle.

questions.prompt: What will you probably need first?
options: Heavier weights for the lower body
Lighter dumbbells for the upper body
A foam roller
A treadmill for fat loss
questions.explanation: Legs and hips outgrow 10–12 kg first.

questions.prompt: In two sentences, explain why lifting matters when you're trying to lose fat.
questions.modelAnswer: In a calorie deficit the body can lose muscle as well as fat. Resistance training signals that the muscle is still needed, so more of the weight lost is fat.

exercises.scenario: A friend cuts 1,000 kcal a day and stops lifting to 'save energy'.

questions.prompt: What's likely?
options: Pure fat loss with all muscle kept, since protein is enough
No change at all
More muscle gained
Faster weight loss with more muscle lost
questions.explanation: Big deficit and no lifting both put muscle at risk.

questions.prompt: What would you suggest?
options: An even bigger deficit for a shorter time
A moderate deficit and 2–3 strength sessions a week
Only stretching and walking
Supplements instead of lifting
questions.explanation: That keeps muscle while fat goes.

summary.title: Combining it all into one goal
points: Cardio and weights do different jobs; together they're best for body composition.
WHO: 150–300 min aerobic a week plus strength on ≥2 days.
Cardio doesn't blunt muscle or max strength; space sessions ≥3 h for explosive strength.
Recomposition is realistic for new lifters with protein and progression.
Set one priority per 12 weeks with outcome, performance and behaviour targets.

exercises.scenario: Your week: football Tuesday, tennis Saturday, 3 × 30 min strength.

questions.prompt: Where do the strength sessions go?
options: Friday, Saturday morning and Sunday
Monday, Thursday and another non-sport day
Straight after football and tennis, so the body is warm
All three on Sunday
questions.explanation: Away from sport, and no hard legs before a match.

questions.prompt: Which target is the one you control directly?
options: Weight down 5 kg
Waist down 4 cm in twelve weeks, measured each month
Three sessions a week
Goblet squat 30 reps
questions.explanation: Behaviour targets.

questions.prompt: Write your own 12-week priority and one target of each kind.
questions.modelAnswer: Example: priority fat loss while keeping and building muscle; outcome waist −3 cm; performance goblet squat 20 → 30 reps at 12 kg; behaviour 3 strength sessions a week plus sport and 8,000+ steps a day.

exercises.scenario: Week 8: weight flat, waist −3 cm, strength up.

questions.prompt: What's happening?
options: Only water changes
Interference from the sport is blocking all fat loss
Nothing; the plan should be scrapped
Recomposition
questions.explanation: Less fat, more muscle, same weight.

questions.prompt: What's the next step in the loop?
options: Keep progressing and review again at week 12
Drop the strength sessions to focus on fat loss
Cut 1,000 kcal a day to make the scale move
Change every exercise
questions.explanation: It's working; keep overload going.

summary.title: Goals and how to combine them: the whole picture
points: Four qualities plus the engine; goals set the emphasis.
Muscle grows across many rep ranges near failure; strength needs heavier loads.
Fat loss: moderate deficit plus lifting, about 0.5–1% of body weight a week.
Cardio and weights complement each other; WHO wants both.
Space strength from sport for explosive power; recomposition is realistic for new lifters.
One priority per 12 weeks, with behaviour targets you control.

exercises.scenario: You design a 12-week plan for fat loss, muscle and strength with sport twice a week.

questions.prompt: What's the weekly core?
options: Daily long runs plus one weights session at the weekend
Seven short HIIT sessions
Only sport, with a strict diet
2–3 full-body strength sessions plus your sport
questions.explanation: Strength for muscle, sport for the engine.

questions.prompt: Which deficit fits?
options: A deficit only on training days
Moderate, losing ~0.5–1% of body weight a week
None at all
As large as you can manage, around 1,000 kcal a day or more
questions.explanation: Large deficits stall muscle gain.

questions.prompt: How do you judge progress at week 4?
options: Behaviour first, then waist, strength and weight trend
How sore you feel
How many calories your watch shows
Weight alone, compared day to day
questions.explanation: Weight can hide recomposition.

exercises.scenario: Your current habit: same weights, same reps, mostly cardio.

questions.prompt: Which change matters most for your goals?
options: More cardio at a higher intensity, because it burns more energy per session
A new watch
Progressive resistance training
Stretching before sport
questions.explanation: Specificity and overload.

questions.prompt: What happens to your sport?
options: It stays as your cardio base, spaced from strength sessions
It has to go, because cardio kills muscle gains
It moves to straight after lifting
It becomes daily
questions.explanation: Interference is small and manageable.

questions.prompt: Summarise your plan for the next 12 weeks in three lines.
questions.modelAnswer: Priority: fat loss while building muscle and strength. Each week: 3 × 30 min full-body strength with progressive overload, sport once or twice spaced from it, a moderate deficit with enough protein and 8,000+ steps. Review at weeks 4, 8 and 12 against the baseline.
